22. Q: How should the crawler search the DOM for the first valid link?
A: Show answer
The crawler should traverse the content tree in a defined order and examine candidate link elements as they are encountered. For each candidate, it should apply the validity rules: the link must be in the relevant article content, must not be excluded by the chosen rules for italics or parentheses, and must not point to an external site or the current page. Depending on the selected variant, it may also exclude red links or links whose text begins with an uppercase letter. The search stops at the first candidate that passes all rules. It should not collect every link and then choose arbitrarily, because the conjecture depends on the first qualifying link in the chosen traversal order.
Study instruction:
- Create a page containing several candidate anchors and mark the first one that passes each rule in sequence.
Key point:
- “First valid link” requires a stable traversal order and explicit validation rules.
- The crawler should stop searching once the first qualifying candidate is found.
Source links:
- Think Dast: Java starting page
23. Q: Why should the crawler restrict its search to the article's content text?
A: Show answer
A Wikipedia page contains navigation, sidebars, boxes, menus, references, and other links that do not necessarily belong to the article's main prose. If the crawler accepts the first anchor anywhere in the document, it may follow a navigation link rather than the link intended by the conjecture. Restricting the search to the content area makes the implementation more faithful to the rule that links should be found in the article text. The chapter's WikiFetcher identifies the element with the mw-content-text ID and selects paragraph elements from it. This provides a starting boundary, although the crawler still needs to decide how to traverse the paragraph descendants and whether every paragraph should be treated equally.
Study instruction:
- Compare the links in a page's navigation and sidebar with links in its main paragraphs, then specify the DOM boundary your crawler will use.
Key point:
- Page-wide link search can select navigation links unrelated to article prose.
- Restricting the search area improves consistency with the conjecture's intended rule.
Source links:
- Think Dast: Java starting page
24. Q: How can a crawler determine whether a link is inside italic text?
A: Show answer
When the traversal reaches an anchor element, the crawler can follow the element's parent links upward through the DOM tree. If any ancestor has an i or em tag, the anchor is inside italicized content under the chapter's suggested rule. The test must inspect the entire relevant ancestor chain, not just the anchor's immediate parent, because the link may be nested inside several elements. The traversal should stop when it reaches the relevant content boundary or the root of the DOM tree. This check is a structural property of the link's location, so it can be implemented as a helper method that receives the anchor and examines its ancestors.
Study instruction:
- Build nested HTML examples with an anchor directly inside i, inside em, and several levels below an italic ancestor; verify that all are classified consistently.
Key point:
- Italic status can be detected by examining ancestor elements for i or em.
- Checking only the immediate parent can miss nested italic formatting.
Source links:
- Think Dast: Java starting page
25. Q: How can the crawler determine whether a link appears inside parentheses?
A: Show answer
Parentheses are a property of the surrounding text sequence rather than an attribute of the anchor element. The chapter suggests scanning the text while traversing the DOM and tracking whether an opening parenthesis has been encountered without a matching closing parenthesis. When an anchor is reached, the crawler can use the current parenthesis state to decide whether the link is inside parentheses. The state must be updated as text nodes are visited in document order. This approach must account for parentheses that begin in one text node and end in another, as well as nested parentheses. A simple Boolean can indicate whether depth is greater than zero, while an integer counter provides a clearer way to handle nesting and unmatched delimiters.
Study instruction:
- Trace a paragraph containing ordinary text, nested parentheses, and links split across several text nodes; record the parenthesis depth at each anchor.
Key point:
- Parenthesis filtering requires state across adjacent text nodes.
- A depth counter handles nested parentheses more reliably than a simple toggle.
Source links:
- Think Dast: Java starting page
26. Q: Why is nested-parenthesis handling important in DOM traversal?
A: Show answer
HTML parsing can split visible text into multiple nodes, and parentheses can open and close at different points in that sequence. If the crawler merely toggles a Boolean every time it sees a parenthesis, nested structures can produce incorrect state. For example, after an outer opening parenthesis and an inner opening parenthesis, closing the inner pair should not make the crawler believe that the text is outside all parentheses. A counter that increments for each opening parenthesis and decrements for each closing parenthesis represents nesting depth. A link is considered inside parentheses when the depth is greater than zero. The implementation should also define how to handle malformed or unmatched parentheses so that a single bad delimiter does not corrupt the rest of the page's processing.
Study instruction:
- Test the strings (A (B) C), A (B) C, and an unmatched opening parenthesis, and explain the state after each character sequence.
Key point:
- Nested delimiters require depth-aware state rather than a simple on/off toggle.
- The crawler should define a predictable policy for malformed text.
Source links:
- Think Dast: Java starting page
27. Q: Why should external links be skipped?
A: Show answer
The conjecture concerns a sequence of Wikipedia article links, so a link to an unrelated external website does not continue the intended process. The crawler should inspect the link destination and determine whether it belongs to the permitted Wikipedia article domain or another allowed internal destination. A text label alone is not sufficient: an anchor that looks like an article title may still point outside Wikipedia. Domain validation should be based on the parsed destination rather than a loose substring test, which can accidentally accept misleading host names. The exact allowed domain and treatment of language-specific Wikipedia hosts should be stated as implementation choices so that the crawler's results can be reproduced and evaluated.
Study instruction:
- Test internal article links, external links, and look-alike host names, and specify a domain-validation rule that cannot be fooled by a simple substring match.
Key point:
- The crawler should follow only destinations permitted by its stated domain rule.
- Host validation should examine the parsed host, not just search the URL text for “wikipedia.”
Source links:
- Think Dast: Java starting page
28. Q: Why should a link to the current page be excluded?
A: Show answer
A link to the current page does not advance the crawler to a new article. If it is selected as the first valid link, the crawler may immediately detect a repeated URL and stop, even though another qualifying link appears later in the page. The chapter therefore recommends skipping links to the current page when selecting the next destination. The comparison should use normalized URLs where appropriate, because two different textual representations can refer to the same page. For example, a relative link and its absolute equivalent may identify the same resource. The crawler should resolve relative destinations against the current page before comparing them, and should define whether fragments or trailing slashes affect page identity.
Study instruction:
- Create examples of absolute, relative, and fragment-bearing links that refer to the current page, then test your normalization and comparison logic.
Key point:
- A self-link does not make progress and should not displace a later candidate.
- Normalize destinations before comparing page identity.
Source links:
- Think Dast: Java starting page
29. Q: Why might red links be excluded from the crawler's valid-link rules?
A: Show answer
In the chapter's description, red links are links to pages that do not yet exist in the relevant Wikipedia context. Following such a link would not continue the intended sequence through existing encyclopedia articles. A crawler may therefore exclude them as part of its definition of a valid link. The implementation should not assume that link color alone is a reliable test, because styling can vary and a visual color may come from CSS rather than the semantic state of the destination. Where the page exposes a reliable structural indicator, the crawler can use that indicator; otherwise, it should document the limitation of its approximation. This rule is one of the optional variations among different versions of the conjecture.

30. Q: Should the crawler skip links whose text begins with an uppercase letter?
A: Show answer
Some versions of the conjecture exclude links whose visible text starts with an uppercase letter, but the chapter presents this as an optional rule rather than a universal requirement. Such a filter may remove links that are proper names or headings, but it can also exclude legitimate article links. Capitalization is a heuristic, not proof that a link is unsuitable. The crawler should therefore make the choice explicit and test how it changes the path. If the goal is to reproduce a particular published version of the conjecture, the relevant capitalization rule must be followed exactly. If the goal is simply to explore the process, the rule can be omitted while the other validity criteria are maintained.

31. Q: How should the crawler decide what to do when a page has no valid link?
A: Show answer
If the traversal reaches the end of the relevant content without finding a qualifying link, the crawler should report failure and stop. It should not invent a destination, choose a link that failed the rules, or repeatedly fetch the same page. The result should distinguish “no valid link found” from network failure, malformed HTML, or a parsing error, because those conditions have different causes and may require different responses. A useful diagnostic records the current URL, the number of candidate links examined, and the reason each candidate was rejected where practical. Clear failure reporting makes the experiment reproducible and helps identify whether the problem lies in the page, the filtering rules, or the crawler implementation.

32. Q: Why should the crawler stop when the selected link has already been visited?
A: Show answer
A repeated URL indicates that the crawler has returned to a page it has already processed. Continuing without a cycle check can cause an infinite loop or repeat the same sequence of pages indefinitely. The chapter explicitly requires failure when the first valid link is a page already seen. The visited collection therefore acts as a record of the crawler's history and a termination safeguard. The check should occur after the next candidate has been resolved to a comparable URL and before it becomes the next current page. The output should identify the repeated destination so that the user can understand where the cycle occurred.

- Create a small graph of pages containing a cycle and trace how the visited-URL check prevents repeated processing.

33. Q: How should the crawler recognize that it has reached the philosophy page?
A: Show answer
The crawler should compare the selected destination with the intended target page and stop successfully when they match. The comparison should use a well-defined representation of the target URL rather than relying only on a visible link label, because text can differ from the actual destination. The chapter says that the program should indicate success when the link matches the URL of the Wikipedia page on philosophy. A robust implementation should resolve relative links, account for redirects where relevant, and define whether a language-specific article or a URL variant counts as the same target. These are implementation decisions that should be documented rather than silently assumed.

34. Q: Why must the crawler record the URLs it visits?
A: Show answer
The visit history serves several purposes. It allows the program to detect cycles, provides evidence of the path taken, and lets the user inspect the result whether the crawler succeeds or fails. The chapter specifically requires building a List of visited URLs and displaying the results at the end. Recording the sequence also helps debug unexpected behavior: if a path diverges from expectations, the programmer can examine which link was selected at each step. The history should record a consistent URL representation and should not silently omit the starting page. If a request fails, the program should distinguish a URL that was attempted from a page that was successfully fetched, if that distinction matters to the report.

35. Q: What is the difference between a visited list and a visited set?
A: Show answer
A list preserves the order in which pages were visited, which is necessary to display the crawler's path. A set supports efficient membership checks to determine whether a destination has already been encountered. The chapter asks for a List because the output should show the sequence of URLs. For a larger crawler, maintaining both a list and a set can be useful: append each newly accepted URL to the list and add it to the set, then use the set to test for cycles. The two structures serve different purposes and should be kept consistent. If only a list is used, membership checks may require scanning earlier entries; if only a set is used, the visit order may not be preserved as required by the report.
Study instruction:
- Design a crawler state object containing both an ordered path and a membership set, and specify when each is updated.
Key point:
- A list preserves path order; a set supports membership checks.
- Combining them can improve clarity and lookup efficiency without losing the reported sequence.
Source links:
- Think Dast: Java starting page
36. Q: How can URL normalization improve cycle detection and target matching?
A: Show answer
The same page can sometimes be represented by different URL strings, such as a relative path and an absolute address, a URL with or without a fragment, or variations in trailing slashes and query parameters. If the crawler compares raw strings, it may treat equivalent destinations as different pages or incorrectly identify distinct resources as identical. Normalization should therefore resolve relative references against the current page and apply a carefully defined canonicalization policy. It should not remove query parameters or fragments indiscriminately, because they can affect resource identity or page behavior. The policy should be consistent for the visited set, current-page comparison, and target-page check so that the crawler does not use conflicting definitions of identity.
Study instruction:
- Create a test table of URL variants and state which should be treated as the same page under your crawler's documented normalization policy.
Key point:
- Raw string equality may not represent page identity reliably.
- Normalize consistently, but preserve URL components that may change the resource.
Source links:
- Think Dast: Java starting page
37. Q: How should the crawler handle relative links found in an article?
A: Show answer
A relative link is interpreted in relation to the page containing it, so it must be resolved against the current page URL before it is fetched or compared with visited URLs. Treating a relative path as a complete URL can cause retrieval errors or incorrect cycle detection. The resolution step should also preserve the correct scheme and host and should then be followed by the crawler's domain and validity checks. It is important to resolve the link before testing whether it points to the current page, an already visited page, or the philosophy target. This makes comparisons operate on meaningful destinations rather than incomplete strings taken directly from an HTML attribute.
Study instruction:
- Resolve several relative link examples against a current article URL and verify the resulting absolute destinations before filtering them.
Key point:
- Resolve relative references before fetching or comparing destinations.
- Domain, cycle, and target checks should use the resolved URL.
Source links:
- Think Dast: Java starting page
38. Q: What is the purpose of the WikiFetcher class?
A: Show answer
WikiFetcher encapsulates the code for downloading Wikipedia pages, parsing the HTML, selecting the content text, and controlling the interval between requests. Its public fetchWikipedia(String url) method returns an Elements collection containing the paragraph elements from the page's content area. By keeping this work in a utility class, the crawler can focus on selecting the next valid link rather than repeating network and parsing code at every step. The class also centralizes request pacing so that the crawler can follow one consistent policy. This separation makes the program easier to understand, test, and maintain, provided that the fetcher is used in the intended way.
Study instruction:
- Identify which responsibilities belong in WikiFetcher and which belong in the crawler's link-selection and termination logic.
Key point:
- WikiFetcher centralizes page retrieval, parsing, content selection, and request pacing.
- The crawler should not duplicate those responsibilities in every iteration.
Source links:
- Think Dast: Java starting page
39. Q: What does WikiFetcher.fetchWikipedia(String url) return?
A: Show answer
The method accepts a URL string, waits if necessary to respect the configured request interval, connects to the URL using Jsoup, downloads and parses the document, finds the element whose ID is mw-content-text, selects its paragraph elements, and returns them as an Elements collection. The returned collection gives the crawler a focused starting point for examining article content. The method declares IOException, which signals that network or input-output problems can occur and must be handled by the calling program. The method's return value is not a complete crawler result; it is the set of paragraph elements that the crawler can traverse to locate the next qualifying link.
Study instruction:
- Trace each operation in fetchWikipedia and describe the type of information available after the method returns.
Key point:
- The fetcher returns paragraph elements selected from the parsed content area.
- Network failures are possible and are represented through IOException.

- Think Dast: Java starting page
40. Q: Why does WikiFetcher select the mw-content-text element and its paragraphs?
A: Show answer
The mw-content-text element provides a boundary around the page's main content area in the chapter's example. Selecting paragraph elements within that boundary reduces the chance that the crawler will start with navigation or sidebar links unrelated to the article's prose. It also gives the link-selection code a manageable collection of content elements to traverse. The exact structure of a live website can change, so the implementation should check that the expected element exists and that paragraph selection returns a usable collection. If the page layout changes, the crawler should report a parsing or structure problem rather than silently treat an empty selection as proof that the article contains no valid links.
Study instruction:
- Inspect the parsed document for the expected content element and test the crawler's behavior when it is absent or contains no paragraphs.
Key point:
- Selecting a content boundary helps exclude navigation and unrelated page regions.
- DOM assumptions should be checked because website structure can change.
Source links:
- Think Dast: Java starting page
41. Q: How does WikiFetcher enforce a minimum interval between requests?
A: Show answer
The class stores lastRequestTime and minInterval, with the example using a default minimum interval of 1,000 milliseconds. Before a request, sleepIfNeeded() calculates the earliest permitted next-request time by adding the minimum interval to the previous request time. If the current time is earlier than that point, the method sleeps for the remaining duration. It then updates lastRequestTime to the current time. This simple mechanism spaces requests made through the same fetcher instance. It is a pacing safeguard, not a guarantee that every request complies with every website policy; the crawler must still respect the site's terms, technical guidance, and any additional limits that apply.
Study instruction:
- Work through a timeline with request times and a 1,000-millisecond minimum interval, calculating how long the next call should wait.
Key point:
- The fetcher enforces a minimum gap between calls made through one instance.
- Request pacing complements, but does not replace, website policy compliance.
Source links:
- Think Dast: Java starting page
42. Q: Why should the crawler use one shared WikiFetcher instance for all requests?
A: Show answer
The chapter warns that multiple WikiFetcher instances do not coordinate their request timestamps. If the crawler creates a new instance for every page, each instance may believe it is making its first request and therefore skip the intended delay. Reusing one instance ensures that the same lastRequestTime state is used across the crawl. The chapter notes that a singleton could prevent accidental creation of multiple independent instances, but a singleton is only one possible design. Passing one fetcher object to the crawler or keeping it as a single owned dependency can also make the intended lifetime explicit without imposing global state on the entire application.
Study instruction:
- Compare a crawler that creates a fetcher inside each loop iteration with one that creates it once before the loop; explain the effect on request timing.
Key point:
- Rate-limit state is shared only when requests use the same fetcher instance.
- Reuse one controlled instance rather than recreating it for every page.
Source links:
- Think Dast: Singleton pattern
- Think Dast: Java starting page
43. Q: What is a singleton, and why does the chapter mention it in relation to WikiFetcher?
A: Show answer
A singleton is a design pattern intended to ensure that a class has one shared instance accessible through a controlled creation mechanism. The chapter mentions it because separate WikiFetcher objects maintain separate lastRequestTime values, so they cannot enforce a single shared request interval across those instances. A singleton could centralize that state. However, a singleton is not automatically the best solution: it can make tests harder, introduce hidden global dependencies, and complicate concurrent use. For this exercise, creating one fetcher and passing it to the crawler may be simpler and clearer. The important requirement is that all requests governed by one rate limit share the same timing state.
Study instruction:
- Compare a singleton with explicit dependency injection of one WikiFetcher instance, including testability and state ownership.
Key point:
- The singleton suggestion addresses shared state, not the crawler's core algorithm.
- One explicitly shared instance can enforce the same interval without requiring global access.
Source links:
- Think Dast: Singleton pattern
44. Q: What are the limitations of the chapter's sleepIfNeeded() implementation?
A: Show answer
The example is deliberately simple. It stores one previous request time and a fixed minimum interval, but it does not by itself coordinate multiple processes, multiple fetcher instances, or requests made by other applications. It also catches InterruptedException, prints a warning, and continues; a production implementation should define how interruption affects the crawl and should preserve the thread's interruption status when appropriate. The timing state is updated using the current time after the sleep check, so actual network completion time and request-start time are not separately recorded. A more robust design may need a configurable interval, better logging, cancellation handling, and a clearly documented definition of when the interval begins.
Study instruction:
- Review the sleepIfNeeded code and identify how it behaves under interruption, concurrent use, multiple instances, and changing rate-limit settings.
Key point:
- The example demonstrates basic pacing, not a complete production rate-limiting system.
- Interruption, concurrency, and shared state require deliberate handling.
Source links:
- Think Dast: Java starting page
- Think Dast: Singleton pattern
45. Q: How should the crawler handle IOException during page retrieval?
A: Show answer
fetchWikipedia declares IOException, so the calling code must decide how retrieval failures affect the crawl. A failed request should not be treated as though the page had no valid link, because the crawler has not successfully inspected the page. The program should report the URL and the nature of the failure, then stop or apply a controlled retry policy. Repeated retries should be limited and should respect the same request pacing and any applicable server instructions. If the crawler stops, it should preserve the path already visited and distinguish a retrieval error from a logical failure such as a repeated URL or missing valid link. This distinction makes the output useful for debugging and honest reporting.
Study instruction:
- Simulate a retrieval exception and verify that the crawler reports a network or I/O failure separately from a no-link result.
Key point:
- A failed fetch is not evidence that a page contains no valid link.
- Error handling should preserve the path and identify the actual failure category.
Source links:
- Think Dast: Java starting page
46. Q: How can a crawler distinguish a parsing problem from a page that has no valid link?
A: Show answer
A parsing problem occurs when the downloaded response cannot be interpreted as expected or the DOM structure required by the program is missing. A no-valid-link result occurs only after the page has been successfully fetched and parsed, the relevant content area has been identified, and all candidate links have been examined under the stated rules. The crawler should therefore validate the response, check that the content element exists, and confirm that traversal completed before declaring that no valid link was found. Logging the current URL, response or parsing status, and rejected-link reasons can make these conditions distinguishable. This avoids reporting a website layout change or malformed response as a failure of the conjecture itself.
Study instruction:
- Create separate tests for an empty article, a missing content element, malformed response data, and a valid page with all links rejected.
Key point:
- No-link is a conclusion after successful parsing and complete candidate evaluation.
- Fetch and parse failures need separate diagnostic outcomes.
Source links:
- Think Dast: Java starting page
47. Q: What practical safeguards should be added before running a crawler against a live website?
A: Show answer
The chapter's one-second delay is a useful reminder that automated retrieval can place load on a server and may violate site terms if performed too aggressively. Before running a crawler, check the website's current terms and crawling guidance, identify any robots directives or published API alternatives, use an appropriate request identity where required, limit the number of requests, and avoid parallel requests that bypass the intended pacing. Stop when the site signals that requests should not continue, and do not attempt to evade access controls or rate limits. The crawler should also use timeouts and bounded error handling so that a failed connection does not create an uncontrolled retry loop. Responsible crawling is part of correct engineering, not an optional courtesy.
Study instruction:
- Prepare a pre-run checklist covering permission, site guidance, request interval, request volume, timeouts, and stop conditions.
Key point:
- A technically working crawler can still be irresponsible or non-compliant.
- Request limits and site instructions must be respected throughout the run.
Source links:
- Think Dast: Java starting page
48. Q: How should the crawler handle a page whose structure changes after the program has been written?
A: Show answer
The crawler should treat its assumptions about page structure as dependencies that can fail. If the expected content element disappears, paragraph selection returns nothing, or link markup changes, the program should produce a diagnostic rather than silently return an incorrect path. The DOM selectors should be isolated in a small component so that they can be updated and tested without rewriting the traversal algorithm. Regression tests using saved representative HTML can help detect structural changes before another live crawl is attempted. The program should also record enough context to identify which selector or assumption failed. This separates a website change from a genuine result of the Getting to Philosophy experiment.
Study instruction:
- Save a small HTML fixture and write tests for the expected content selector, paragraph selection, and link extraction so that layout changes can be detected.
Key point:
- DOM selectors are assumptions that should be checked and tested.
- Isolating parsing rules makes website changes easier to diagnose and maintain.
Source links:
- Think Dast: Java starting page
49. Q: How can the crawler be tested without repeatedly downloading live Wikipedia pages?
A: Show answer
Most algorithmic behavior can be tested with small saved HTML documents or constructed DOM trees. Test fixtures can represent a page with one valid link, several rejected links before a valid link, nested parentheses, an italic ancestor, an external destination, a self-link, a repeated destination, and no qualifying link. The crawler's selection logic can be separated from the network fetcher so that tests supply prepared DOM content without making HTTP requests. Live tests can then be limited to a small number of controlled checks that respect request pacing. This approach makes tests faster, more deterministic, and less dependent on changing website content or network availability.
Study instruction:
- Design a fixture for each validity rule and run the selection logic against the fixtures before conducting a limited live test.
Key point:
- Unit tests should verify link-selection logic without requiring live network access.
- Live tests should be limited and paced responsibly.
Source links:
- Think Dast: Java starting page
50. Q: What should the crawler report when it reaches the end of a run?
A: Show answer
The chapter requires the program to build a List of visited URLs and display the results whether the crawler succeeds or fails. A useful report should show the starting URL, the ordered sequence of pages visited, the final URL or attempted destination, and a clear outcome such as target reached, no valid link, repeated page, or retrieval failure. Where possible, it should also explain the link-selection rules used, because different rule variants can produce different paths. The report should not claim success merely because the loop ended; success is specific to reaching the defined philosophy target. Clear output makes the experiment reproducible and allows the reader to investigate unexpected results.
Study instruction:
- Define a result format that includes the ordered URL path, terminal condition, and link-filtering configuration.
Key point:
- A completed run must report both its path and why it stopped.
- Success and failure should be explicit, not inferred from loop termination.
Source links:
- Think Dast: Java starting page
51. Q: How can the crawler avoid choosing a link that passes one rule but fails another?
A: Show answer
Link validation should be implemented as a clear sequence of checks or a single well-defined predicate. For each anchor, the program should verify that it is within the allowed content region, has a usable destination, is not external under the chosen domain rule, is not a self-link, is not inside excluded italic or parenthetical content, and satisfies any optional red-link or capitalization rule. The order of checks can affect performance and diagnostic messages, but the final decision should be consistent. Keeping each rule in a named helper method makes the code easier to review and test. The crawler should also record rejection reasons during debugging so that a surprising choice can be traced to a specific rule.
Study instruction:
- Implement separate validation methods and test each rule independently before combining them into the final candidate-selection predicate.
Key point:
- A valid link must pass every rule in the chosen definition.
- Modular checks make filtering logic easier to verify and maintain.
Source links:
- Think Dast: Java starting page
52. Q: How should the crawler handle links whose destination is missing or malformed?
A: Show answer
An anchor may have no destination attribute, an empty destination, or a value that cannot be interpreted as a valid URI. Such a candidate should not be followed. The crawler should treat it as a rejected link and continue searching for the next candidate, provided that doing so is consistent with the chosen “first valid link” definition. It should distinguish malformed destinations from external destinations and self-links because each rejection has a different cause. Parsing should be performed with a URI-aware mechanism rather than assuming every attribute value is a complete URL. If all candidates are rejected, the crawler can then report that no valid link was found, with diagnostic information available for investigation.
Study instruction:
- Test anchors with missing, empty, malformed, relative, and absolute destination values and specify how each should be handled.
Key point:
- Missing or malformed destinations should not be fetched.
- URI parsing and explicit rejection reasons make link selection more reliable.
Source links:
- Think Dast: Java starting page
53. Q: What is the difference between the crawler's link-selection order and the order of URLs in its visit history?
A: Show answer
Link-selection order is the order in which DOM nodes and candidate anchors are examined while searching for the next destination. Visit-history order is the sequence of page URLs actually accepted and followed by the crawler. They are related but not identical: many anchors may be examined and rejected on one page before a single URL is added to the visit history. Confusing these sequences can lead to incorrect debugging, because the visit list does not show every candidate considered. If detailed diagnostics are needed, the crawler can separately log rejected candidates and the reason for each rejection, while keeping the visit history focused on pages actually followed.
Study instruction:
- For one sample page, record candidate examination order separately from the sequence of URLs that the crawler actually visits.
Key point:
- Candidate order describes the search within a page; visit order describes the crawl path.
- Separate logs avoid confusing rejected links with visited pages.
Source links:
- Think Dast: Java starting page
54. Q: How can the crawler be organized into components that are easier to maintain?
A: Show answer
A maintainable design can separate page fetching, DOM traversal, link validation, URL normalization, crawl-state management, and result reporting. WikiFetcher already provides a boundary for network retrieval and paragraph selection. WikiNodeIterable and WikiNodeIterator provide a reusable traversal mechanism. Additional helpers can determine whether a candidate is in italics or parentheses, whether its destination is permitted, and whether it has already been visited. A crawl controller can coordinate the repeated fetch-and-follow loop, while a result object stores the ordered path and terminal outcome. This organization makes it possible to change a filtering rule or parsing selector without rewriting the entire application.
Study instruction:
- Draw a component diagram showing the responsibilities and data passed between fetcher, DOM iterator, validator, crawl controller, and result reporter.
Key point:
- Small components isolate network, traversal, validation, state, and reporting concerns.
- Clear boundaries make changes and tests more manageable.
Source links:
- Think Dast: Iterable interface
- Think Dast: Iterator interface
55. Q: What assumptions and limitations should be documented when interpreting the crawler's result?
A: Show answer
The result depends on the starting page, the version of the page retrieved, the content selector, the traversal order, the definition of a valid link, URL normalization, and the state of the site during the run. The chapter notes that the example path from the Java page reached Philosophy after seven links unless something had changed since the author ran it. That qualification matters: Wikipedia content and markup can change, and different valid-link rules can produce different sequences. A failed run does not necessarily disprove every version of the conjecture; it may show that the implementation's chosen rules, starting page, or current page content produced a different outcome. The report should therefore state its assumptions and avoid overgeneralizing from one execution.
Study instruction:
- Write a short experiment note recording the start page, retrieval date, link rules, software assumptions, and terminal result.
Key point:
- A crawl result is conditional on the rules and page state used in the experiment.
- One execution should not be treated as proof of a universal claim.

Rows: 55
Table 8
Indexing Web Content: Term Frequency, Inverted Indexes, and Search Operations
1. Q: What is the purpose of an index in a web-search system?
A: Show answer
An index is a data structure that lets a search system move from a search term to the pages containing that term without repeatedly examining every page in the collection. It can also retain the number of times the term occurs on each page. The first capability identifies candidate pages; the frequency information provides evidence that may help distinguish pages where the term is prominent from pages where it appears only incidentally. The chapter's design is an inverted index: instead of storing each page as the primary route to all its words, it stores each term as a key associated with the pages in which that term occurs. This changes the main search operation from scanning page text to looking up a term and retrieving its posting set.
Study instruction:
- Explain the direction of an inverted index and trace how one query term leads to a collection of matching pages.
Key point:
- An index maps terms to pages and supports efficient retrieval.
- Per-page term counts add information beyond simple page membership.
2. Q: What makes the chapter's index an inverted index?
A: Show answer
The index is inverted because its primary lookup direction is from a word to the documents that contain it. A page-oriented representation starts with a page and lists its terms; an inverted representation starts with a term and lists the pages associated with that term. In the chapter, an Index maps a search term to a Set of TermCounter objects. Each TermCounter represents one page and records the frequencies of terms on that page. This arrangement is suited to search because a query begins with terms supplied by the user. The system can retrieve the page sets for those terms and combine them, rather than opening every page and testing its text from the beginning.
Study instruction:
- Draw both a page-to-terms representation and a term-to-pages representation, then explain why the second better supports term lookup.
Key point:
- The inverted direction matches the way a search query is expressed.
- Each term's posting set identifies the pages that contain it.
3. Q: Why would searching every page's text for every query term be inefficient?
A: Show answer
A direct-scan approach would visit the contents of the pages and test whether each page contains the requested term. Its work grows with the total amount of text that must be examined, not merely with the number of matching pages. As the collection grows, repeated scans perform much of the same work for different queries. An index pays a cost when pages are processed and stored, then reuses the resulting term-to-page associations for later searches. This is a preprocessing-versus-query trade-off: maintaining the index consumes storage and requires update work, but it avoids repeatedly scanning the full corpus for common lookups. The chapter therefore chooses a Map-based lookup structure rather than a collection of raw pages as the basic search mechanism.
Study instruction:
- Compare the work required by a full text scan with the work required to retrieve an already-built posting set for a term.
Key point:
- Repeated full scans redo work for every query.
- Index construction moves much of that work into a reusable preprocessing stage.
4. Q: What is a Map, and why is it appropriate for looking up search terms?
A: Show answer
A Map represents key-value pairs. A caller supplies a key and retrieves the value associated with it; in the chapter's design, a search term is the key and a count or collection of pages is the value. The important operations introduced are get(key), which looks up the associated value, and put(key, value), which adds a new pair or replaces the value for an existing key. This abstraction directly expresses the index's main operation: given a term, find its information. A Map also separates the intended behavior from the concrete implementation, allowing the program to use a HashMap or TreeMap without changing the conceptual key-value relationship.
Study instruction:
- For each Map in the chapter, identify its key type, value type, and the exact question answered by get(key).
Key point:
- A Map associates each key with a value.
- The choice of implementation is separate from the Map abstraction.
5. Q: What information does a TermCounter store?
A: Show answer
A TermCounter stores the frequency of each search term in one page. Its map field associates a String term with an Integer count, while its label field identifies the page from which the counts were obtained. The label is intended to hold the page URL, so a search result can identify not only that a term occurs but also which page contains it. A TermCounter is therefore page-specific: it is not the whole search index. It is the per-document frequency record that the larger Index can collect and retrieve. Keeping these responsibilities separate makes the overall design easier to reason about and allows the same TermCounter structure to be used for each crawled page.
Study instruction:
- Sketch a TermCounter for a short sample page and label the term-frequency map separately from the page identifier.
Key point:
- One TermCounter describes the terms and counts for one page.
- The label connects those counts to the page's URL or other identifier.
6. Q: Why does TermCounter keep a label in addition to its term-count map?
A: Show answer
The counts alone do not identify the page to which they belong. The label supplies that context. In the web-crawler example, the label is the URL used to fetch the page. When the Index later returns TermCounter objects for a search term, the application can use each object's label to show or otherwise identify the matching page. The label is not another search term and should not be confused with a count. It is metadata describing the document represented by the counter. A robust implementation should keep the identifier consistent with the page whose text was actually processed, because a correct frequency attached to the wrong URL would produce a misleading search result.
Study instruction:
- Trace a page URL from the crawler into the TermCounter constructor and then into the display of a matching search result.
Key point:
- The label links document-level statistics to a specific page.
- Correct page identity is essential to trustworthy search results.
7. Q: Why does TermCounter.get return zero when a term has not yet been counted?
A: Show answer
The underlying Map returns null when it has no value for the requested key. TermCounter.get checks that result and returns zero when the term is absent. This gives callers a numeric default that represents an observed frequency of zero, rather than requiring every caller to handle null separately. It simplifies the increment operation: the current count can be read, increased, and stored whether the term is new or already present. The distinction still matters conceptually: zero means the term has not been recorded in this page's counter; it does not mean that the global index has searched every possible page and proved the word never occurs anywhere.
Study instruction:
- Follow the get method for both a present term and an absent term, and explain the difference between null in the Map and zero returned by TermCounter.
Key point:
- The wrapper converts a missing Map value into a usable zero count.
- A page-level zero is not proof that a term is absent from the whole corpus.
8. Q: How does incrementTermCount update a term's frequency?
A: Show answer
incrementTermCount obtains the current count through get(term), adds one, and passes the new value to put(term, count). For a term not previously seen, get supplies zero, so the first occurrence is stored as one. For a term already present, the existing count is increased by one. The method centralizes the counting rule and avoids duplicating the missing-key check in the text-processing loop. Its correctness depends on the get method's zero default and on put replacing the old value for the same key. If the method were changed to increment a different key or to add one to a null value, the frequency record would become incorrect or fail at runtime.
Study instruction:
- Manually trace the counts produced by the sequence “map map index” and verify the stored frequency after each token.
Key point:
- A new term starts at one; each later occurrence adds one.
- get, addition, and put form the complete update cycle.
9. Q: What is the role of the put method in TermCounter?
A: Show answer
TermCounter.put is a wrapper around the put operation of its internal Map. It gives users of TermCounter a simple method for recording a term count without exposing the internal map directly. The wrapper does not introduce a separate counting rule; it delegates storage to the Map, where a new key-value pair is inserted or the value for an existing key is replaced. The distinction between put and incrementTermCount is important: put stores a supplied count, whereas incrementTermCount calculates the next count from the current value. Keeping the wrapper small preserves encapsulation while allowing the class to control how its internal representation is accessed.
Study instruction:
- Compare a direct call to put(term, 7) with seven calls to incrementTermCount(term), and explain when each operation is appropriate.
Key point:
- put stores the count supplied by the caller.
- incrementTermCount derives and stores the next count.
10. Q: What text-processing steps does TermCounter.processText perform?
A: Show answer
processText transforms a text string into tokens and increments the count for each token. The chapter's sequence replaces punctuation characters with spaces, converts the resulting text to lowercase, splits it on one or more whitespace characters, and loops through the resulting array. Each token is passed to incrementTermCount. The order matters: punctuation is treated as a boundary, case differences are normalized, and whitespace separates tokens. This is a simple tokenization pipeline rather than a complete linguistic analysis system. It gives the index a consistent representation for ordinary word matching, but it does not by itself handle stemming, synonyms, stop-word removal, language-specific morphology, or every Unicode normalization issue.
Study instruction:
- Apply each transformation in order to a sample sentence and write down the exact token array that the method would produce.
Key point:
- Text is normalized before frequencies are updated.
- Tokenization rules determine what the index considers the same term.
11. Q: Why does the chapter replace punctuation with spaces instead of simply deleting punctuation?
A: Show answer
Replacing punctuation with spaces preserves a boundary between words that punctuation separates. If punctuation were deleted without adding a separator, two adjacent words could be joined into a token that never appeared in the original text. For example, deleting a comma from “data,structures” could produce “datastructures,” whereas replacing it with a space produces two tokens. The chapter uses a regular-expression replacement to turn punctuation characters into spaces before splitting the text. This is a deliberate token-boundary decision. The exact behavior depends on the punctuation definition used by the regular expression, so the rule should be tested against the languages and document formats the search system is expected to process.
Study instruction:
- Test punctuation deletion and punctuation-to-space replacement on words separated by commas, periods, hyphens, and parentheses.
Key point:
- A separator should remain a separator after normalization.
- Token boundaries directly affect frequency counts and search matches.
12. Q: Why does processText convert terms to lowercase?
A: Show answer
Lowercasing reduces case-based duplication. Without normalization, “Java,” “JAVA,” and “java” could be stored as separate keys even when the search application intends to treat them as the same search term. Converting text to lowercase before counting makes the stored keys more consistent and makes ordinary case-insensitive matching easier. This is a design choice, not a universal rule for every search domain. Some systems must preserve case-sensitive identifiers, programming-language symbols, product codes, or names. A production system should therefore define its case policy explicitly and apply the same policy to both indexed content and user queries. If indexing and query normalization differ, correct pages may fail to match.
Study instruction:
- Compare the tokens generated from “Java JAVA java” before and after lowercasing, then decide whether case-sensitive terms matter in a proposed search domain.
Key point:
- Lowercasing merges case variants under one key.
- Query processing must use a compatible normalization policy.
13. Q: What is the purpose of splitting normalized text on one or more whitespace characters?
A: Show answer
After punctuation has been replaced and case has been normalized, whitespace provides the boundaries used to divide the text into individual tokens. The regular expression for one or more whitespace characters allows a run of spaces, tabs, or line breaks to act as one delimiter rather than creating many empty tokens. This makes the tokenizer more tolerant of ordinary formatting differences in extracted web text. The resulting array is then traversed and each token is counted. A robust implementation should still consider empty input, leading or trailing whitespace, and any empty token behavior of the chosen split operation, because those details can affect counts if they are not handled deliberately.
Study instruction:
- Test the split expression on text containing repeated spaces, tabs, newlines, and leading or trailing whitespace.
Key point:
- Whitespace separates tokens after normalization.
- Consistent splitting prevents formatting differences from distorting counts.
14. Q: What does TermCounter.processElements do?
A: Show answer
processElements receives an Elements collection containing jsoup elements, such as the paragraph elements selected from a web page. It iterates through that collection and calls processTree for each element. It therefore acts as the bridge between a collection of selected HTML elements and the lower-level routine that extracts text from each element's DOM subtree. It does not itself count individual words; that work is delegated through processTree and processText. Separating these stages keeps the code organized: one method handles the collection, another handles traversal of a tree, and another handles tokenization and counting. This division also makes each step easier to test and maintain.
Study instruction:
- Draw the call sequence from processElements to processTree to processText and identify the input type passed at each stage.
Key point:
- processElements iterates the selected page elements.
- It delegates tree traversal and token counting to other methods.
15. Q: Why does processTree traverse a DOM tree instead of reading only the root node's direct text?
A: Show answer
HTML content is nested. A paragraph or other selected element can contain child elements and deeper descendants whose text is part of the visible content. Reading only the root node's direct text could omit words held inside nested nodes. processTree uses WikiNodeIterable to visit nodes in the DOM subtree and checks for TextNode instances. It then extracts text from those nodes and passes it to processText. This makes text extraction recursive in effect: the traversal covers the tree structure rather than assuming all relevant text is stored directly on the root element. Correct traversal is necessary for a counter that is intended to represent the text contained in the selected page content.
Study instruction:
- Sketch a nested HTML fragment and trace which text would be missed by examining only the root element rather than traversing descendants.
Key point:
- Relevant text may occur at multiple depths in a DOM tree.
- Traversal must reach text nodes throughout the selected subtree.
16. Q: What is a TextNode, and why does processTree check for it?
A: Show answer
A TextNode represents text within the document object model rather than an HTML element that describes structure or markup. processTree traverses the nodes under a root and processes only nodes that are TextNode instances. For each such node, it obtains the text and sends it to processText. This avoids trying to tokenize structural nodes as if they were ordinary text. The approach separates document structure from document content: the DOM traversal finds the text-bearing parts, and the tokenizer turns their contents into searchable terms. The choice also means that the crawler's indexing behavior depends on which subtree is traversed and which node types are selected for processing.
Study instruction:
- Distinguish element nodes from text nodes in a small DOM example and identify exactly which values should enter the tokenizer.
Key point:
- TextNode identifies content to be tokenized.
- DOM structure guides extraction but is not itself counted as a word.
17. Q: How do processElements, processTree, and processText work together?
A: Show answer
The three methods form a layered processing pipeline. processElements iterates through the selected jsoup Elements collection. For each element, processTree traverses its DOM subtree and identifies TextNode objects. Each text node's content is passed to processText, which normalizes the text, splits it into tokens, and calls incrementTermCount for each token. The resulting TermCounter map contains the accumulated frequencies for the page. This separation allows the program to change how page elements are selected without rewriting tokenization, or to change tokenization without rewriting the DOM traversal. It also makes troubleshooting more systematic because a missing word can be traced to selection, traversal, normalization, splitting, or counting.
Study instruction:
- For a token that is missing from an index, list the checks you would perform at each stage of this pipeline.
Key point:
- Selection, traversal, tokenization, and counting are separate responsibilities.
- A defect at any stage can produce an incorrect index.
18. Q: Why does the indexer process selected paragraph elements rather than treating every part of an HTML page as searchable text?
A: Show answer
A web page contains more than its main prose. It can include navigation, menus, scripts, style information, advertisements, repeated page furniture, and other text that may be less useful for the search purpose. The example obtains paragraph elements from the page and processes those selected elements. This is a scope decision: the crawler determines which content is eligible for indexing before the TermCounter counts its words. The selection rule affects search quality because omitted relevant content cannot be found, while irrelevant or repeated content can distort frequencies. A real system should define and test its extraction scope, including how it handles headings, captions, metadata, and dynamically generated content.
Study instruction:
- Compare the text in a page's main content with its navigation and footer, then propose a consistent extraction policy for a search application.
Key point:
- Index quality depends on which page regions are selected.
- Text extraction policy is part of search-system design.
19. Q: What is the structure of the Index class introduced in the chapter?
A: Show answer
Index contains a Map from String terms to Set values. Each key is a search term, and its value is the set of page-specific counters for pages in which that term appears. Each TermCounter in turn maps terms to their counts for one page and stores a label identifying that page. The resulting structure has two levels: the outer Map locates the pages associated with a term, and the inner TermCounter maps provide frequency information for those pages. This design supports both membership queries and retrieval of term counts. It also separates the global relationship between terms and pages from the local statistics maintained for each page.
Study instruction:
- Draw the nested Index-to-Map-to-Set-to-TermCounter structure and annotate the type and purpose of every level.
Key point:
- Index maps each term to a set of page counters.
- Each page counter stores that page's term frequencies and identifier.
20. Q: Why does Index map each term to a Set of TermCounter objects rather than to a single TermCounter?
A: Show answer
A search term can appear on many pages. A single TermCounter would represent only one page and would be unable to preserve all matching documents. A Set provides a collection of page counters associated with the term. The Index can therefore return every page represented in the posting set for a query term. The set also expresses the intended collection semantics: the value is a group of distinct page-counter objects, not one count or one document. If the application needs a particular ordering, it must choose or apply an ordering strategy separately; the essential requirement at this stage is to collect the pages that contain the term.
Study instruction:
- Model a term that occurs on three pages and explain why the corresponding Index value must hold all three page counters.
Key point:
- One term can be associated with many pages.
- A set provides the collection of page counters for that term.
21. Q: How does Index.add handle a term that appears for the first time?
A: Show answer
Index.add first calls get(term) to see whether a set is already associated with the term. If the result is null, the term has not yet been entered in the outer index. The method then creates a new HashSet, inserts that set into the index map under the term, and adds the supplied TermCounter to it. Creating the set before adding the page establishes the value needed for future occurrences. The order is significant: the new set must be stored in the map so that later calls can retrieve and extend the same collection. The method therefore initializes a posting set lazily when the first page containing a term is indexed.
Study instruction:
- Trace Index.add for a previously unseen term and identify when the new set is created, stored, and populated.
Key point:
- A new term requires a new posting set.
- The first page counter is added to that set after it is stored in the Map.
22. Q: What happens when Index.add receives a term that already has a posting set?
A: Show answer
When get(term) returns an existing set, Index.add does not need to create a replacement set or reinsert the Map entry. It calls set.add(tc) on the collection already stored as the value for that key. Because the retrieved set is the same mutable object referenced by the Map, adding the TermCounter changes the collection held by the index. This is the distinction the chapter emphasizes: the outer Map is modified when a new term requires a new set, while an existing set can be modified directly. Understanding object references prevents unnecessary map updates and helps explain why a nested mutable collection can be updated through a value retrieved from a Map.
Study instruction:
- Trace a second page containing an existing term and explain why modifying the retrieved set also updates the collection visible through Index.get(term).
Key point:
- Existing posting sets can be extended in place.
- A new Map entry is needed only when the term has no set yet.
23. Q: What does the Set interface contribute to the index design?
A: Show answer
Set represents a collection in which adding an element already present has no effect. The chapter identifies add(element) and contains(element) as core operations. These operations suit a posting collection because the index needs to record which page counters are associated with a term and test membership when required. The Set abstraction also supports set operations such as intersection, even though the interface does not provide a dedicated intersection method in the example. The programmer can implement intersection by using membership checks or by using an appropriate collection operation. Choosing Set communicates that the collection represents distinct members rather than a sequence where repeated occurrences of the same member are meaningful.
Study instruction:
- Explain the difference between storing term frequency in a TermCounter and storing page membership in a Set of TermCounter objects.
Key point:
- Set models distinct members and supports membership-oriented operations.
- Frequency belongs in the page counter, not in duplicate copies of a posting entry.
24. Q: How does set intersection help combine the results of multiple search terms?
A: Show answer
The intersection of two sets contains only elements that appear in both sets. If one posting set contains pages with “Java” and another contains pages with “programming,” their intersection contains pages represented in both sets. This operation implements an AND-style search: a page is retained only if it matches every required term. The chapter uses this relationship to explain why Set is appropriate for the index. A system can retrieve the posting sets for the individual terms and combine them to narrow the candidate pages. The order and implementation of the intersection can affect efficiency, but the logical result is the same: only shared page entries remain.
Study instruction:
- Given two small posting sets, calculate their intersection manually and identify which pages satisfy both terms.
Key point:
- Intersection retains elements common to every input set.
- It provides the basis for multi-term AND queries.
25. Q: How would the index answer a search for pages containing both “Java” and “programming”?
A: Show answer
The system would retrieve the posting set associated with “Java” and the posting set associated with “programming,” then compute their intersection. Pages that occur in both sets are candidates because they contain both terms. This narrows the results compared with returning every page containing either word. The chapter uses the example to show how intersection can reduce irrelevant matches: “Java” alone may refer to the island, coffee, or programming language, while “programming” alone can refer to many languages. Requiring both terms makes the result more focused, although it does not guarantee that every retained page is relevant in the user's intended sense.
Study instruction:
- Create two posting sets for the example terms and calculate the pages that remain after intersection.
Key point:
- A two-term AND query uses the intersection of the two posting sets.
- Shared term membership improves focus but does not itself provide a full ranking model.
26. Q: How does an OR-style search differ from the intersection operation described in the chapter?
A: Show answer
An AND-style search retains pages that occur in every required posting set, which is set intersection. An OR-style search would retain pages that occur in at least one posting set, which is set union. The chapter specifically explains intersection as the operation needed to find pages containing multiple terms together. Union is a related set operation that broadens rather than narrows the candidate collection. A search application must define which behavior its query syntax requires; silently substituting union for intersection would change the meaning of the search. The distinction also matters when users combine terms with explicit Boolean operators or when a system interprets multiple words as alternatives rather than simultaneous requirements.
Study instruction:
- Use the same two posting sets to calculate both intersection and union, then explain how the two result sets answer different queries.
Key point:
- Intersection means all specified sets; union means at least one set.
- Query semantics must determine which operation is used.
27. Q: What should happen when the Index has no posting set for a queried term?
A: Show answer
If Index.get(term) returns null, the term has no entry in the current index. For an AND query that requires this term, the result should be empty because no indexed page is known to contain every required term. The application should handle the missing set explicitly rather than attempting to iterate over null. It should also distinguish a genuinely absent term from an indexing failure or stale index. A missing entry may mean the word does not occur in the indexed corpus, but it could also mean the crawler did not fetch a relevant page or the tokenizer normalized the query differently from the page text. Error handling and consistent normalization are therefore important to interpreting empty results correctly.
Study instruction:
- Design a query path for an unknown term and identify where the application should return an empty result instead of dereferencing null.
Key point:
- A missing posting set should be handled deliberately.
- Empty results can reflect corpus coverage or normalization problems, not only user error.
28. Q: How are Index, TermCounter, Map, and Set related in the chapter's object structure?
A: Show answer
Index owns an outer Map whose keys are terms and whose values are Sets of TermCounter objects. Each Set contains the page counters for pages where its term occurs. Each TermCounter owns another Map from terms to counts and a label identifying the page. The outer Map answers “which pages contain this term?” while the inner Map answers “how many times does this term occur on this page?” The Set groups multiple page counters under one term. This nested arrangement is more expressive than a single flat collection because it separates global search lookup, page membership, and page-specific frequency. Understanding the levels is essential when tracing updates or debugging incorrect results.
Study instruction:
- Recreate the object diagram for one term appearing on two pages and label both the global posting relationship and the local frequency records.
Key point:
- The outer Map locates page sets by term.
- Each TermCounter supplies page identity and per-term frequencies.
29. Q: What does Index.printIndex demonstrate about traversing the data structure?
A: Show answer
printIndex uses a nested iteration. The outer loop visits the search terms, and the inner loop visits the TermCounter objects in the set associated with each term. For each page counter, it retrieves the frequency of the current term and prints the page label and count. This demonstrates how to unpack the nested structure to produce a readable term-to-page listing. It also illustrates why both levels are necessary: iterating only the outer Map would reveal terms but not the pages, while iterating only a page counter would reveal local counts but not the global posting relationships. The method is a diagnostic display, not a complete search-ranking or user-interface implementation.
Study instruction:
- Trace the two loops for a term associated with two pages and state which object supplies the term, page URL, and frequency at each step.
Key point:
- The outer loop traverses terms; the inner loop traverses matching pages.
- The count is read from the page-specific TermCounter.
30. Q: How should a programmer choose between HashMap and TreeMap for this index?
A: Show answer
The chapter identifies HashMap and TreeMap as Map implementations and notes that their performance will be analyzed later. The choice should be based on the operations and behavior the application requires. A hash-based map is commonly selected when fast key lookup is the priority and sorted key iteration is not required. A tree-based map maintains keys in sorted order and can be useful when ordered traversal or range-oriented operations matter. The chapter's initial implementation uses HashMap for TermCounter and Index. A production decision should also consider key comparison rules, expected collection size, update patterns, memory overhead, and the need for predictable ordering rather than assuming that one implementation is universally superior.
Study instruction:
- Compare the application's need for lookup speed with any requirement to display terms in sorted order before choosing a Map implementation.
Key point:
- HashMap and TreeMap implement the same Map abstraction with different behavior and trade-offs.
- Select an implementation according to actual access and ordering requirements.
31. Q: What is the practical distinction between HashSet and TreeSet in the index?
A: Show answer
The chapter lists HashSet and TreeSet as implementations of the Set interface and uses HashSet when creating a posting set. A HashSet is appropriate when membership and insertion are the main concerns and sorted iteration is unnecessary. A TreeSet maintains elements in sorted order according to its ordering rules, which may be useful if the application requires a predictable ordered traversal. The set abstraction remains the same: it represents distinct members and supports operations such as add and contains. The choice of implementation should follow the required behavior and the element comparison or equality rules. The chapter does not require sorted page results, so HashSet is a reasonable simple choice for the exercise.
Study instruction:
- Identify whether a search-result display requires ordering; if it does, specify the ordering key before selecting a set implementation.
Key point:
- HashSet prioritizes hash-based membership behavior; TreeSet provides sorted ordering.
- Ordering requirements should be explicit rather than assumed.
32. Q: Why should the design distinguish term frequency from page membership?
A: Show answer
Page membership answers whether a page contains a term; term frequency answers how many times it occurs on that page. The Index's Set of TermCounter objects represents membership across pages, while each TermCounter's Map stores the frequency for a particular page. Treating these as separate facts prevents the data structure from confusing “this page contains the word” with “this page contains the word a particular number of times.” The distinction is useful for both correctness and later search features. A page can belong to a posting set because its count is positive, while the count itself can be used as one signal when evaluating the page. The chapter does not prescribe a complete relevance formula.
Study instruction:
- For three pages, record both a yes/no membership value and a numeric frequency for the same term, then identify where each belongs in the structure.
Key point:
- The Set records which pages contain a term.
- TermCounter records how frequently the term occurs on each page.
33. Q: What work should Index.indexPage perform when a new page is crawled?
A: Show answer
indexPage receives a page URL and the selected paragraph Elements. Its first responsibility is to create a TermCounter for that page, using the URL as the label. It then processes the supplied elements so the counter contains the terms and frequencies found in the page text. Finally, it iterates through the terms in that counter and adds the TermCounter to the Index for each term. The chapter leaves this method as an exercise, but its comments specify this two-stage logic: count the terms for the page, then connect the page counter to every term in the global index. This method is the integration point between page extraction and the global search structure.
Study instruction:
- Write pseudocode for indexPage and verify that it creates one page counter, processes the selected text, and adds that counter once for every distinct term.
Key point:
- indexPage builds the page-level frequency record before updating global postings.
- Every term in the page counter must be connected to that page in Index.
34. Q: Why does indexPage iterate through the terms in a TermCounter after counting the page?
A: Show answer
The TermCounter contains the set of distinct term keys observed in the page, together with their frequencies. Index needs to associate the page with each term that occurs in it. Iterating through those keys lets indexPage call Index.add(term, tc) for each term. The same TermCounter can be added to several posting sets because it represents the complete term-frequency record for that page. This avoids creating a separate page object for every word. It also keeps the update logic aligned with the index's structure: each term receives a reference to the page counter, and the page counter retains the frequencies for all terms on that page.
Study instruction:
- Given a TermCounter with four distinct term keys, list the four Index.add calls required to index the page.
Key point:
- The page counter's keys determine which posting sets must be updated.
- One TermCounter can be referenced by many term-specific sets.
35. Q: What is the purpose of the TermCounter.size exercise, and why does the initial output show a value of -1?
A: Show answer
The exercise demonstrates how an incomplete method can leave a program's output incorrect even when the surrounding counting logic is working. The example run prints term counts and then reports a total of -1 because the size method has not yet been completed. The learner must implement the missing method so it returns the total of the term counts held by the TermCounter. The key is to distinguish the number of distinct keys from the sum of their frequencies: a total frequency count requires adding the stored count values, not merely counting how many different terms exist. The chapter's test then checks whether the implementation behaves as expected.
Study instruction:
- Implement the total-frequency calculation and test it with a counter containing repeated and distinct terms.
Key point:
- Total occurrences and number of distinct terms are different measurements.
- The incomplete method's -1 is a signal to implement and test the missing logic.
36. Q: Why does the chapter state that the completed TermCounter size calculation should produce 4,798 in the exercise?
A: Show answer
The value 4,798 is the expected total for the particular page content and exercise data used in the chapter. It serves as a test expectation: after the learner implements size correctly and runs the example again, the sum of all term frequencies should equal that value. It is not a universal property of TermCounter, a fixed limit, or a value that every page should produce. Different pages and different extraction rules will produce different totals. The useful lesson is to use a known expected result to validate the implementation and to investigate discrepancies by checking page selection, DOM traversal, tokenization, and increment logic.
Study instruction:
- Reproduce the exercise's test data and explain why the expected total is specific to that input rather than to the class design.
Key point:
- 4,798 is an exercise-specific expected result.
- Test values validate one defined input and should not be generalized to other pages.
37. Q: What does the exercise's use of automated tests contribute to implementing TermCounter and Index?
A: Show answer
The exercise provides test classes for the TermCounter and Index implementations. Tests help determine whether the completed methods behave as intended and make errors reproducible. For TermCounter, tests can check that terms are counted, missing terms return zero, and totals are calculated correctly. For Index, tests can check that terms are associated with the correct page counters and that lookups return the expected collections. Running tests after filling in a missing method is more reliable than judging correctness from one printed example. Tests also support later changes by revealing whether an implementation change has broken behavior that previously worked.
Study instruction:
- Design at least one normal case, one missing-term case, and one repeated-term case for TermCounter, then define expected results for each.
Key point:
- Tests turn intended behavior into repeatable checks.
- A successful sample run is useful but does not replace focused tests.
38. Q: Why does the chapter instruct the learner to run the build before running the TermCounter and Index exercises?
A: Show answer
The build step compiles the source files so that the exercise programs and their dependencies are available for execution. The chapter uses Ant commands to build the project and then run specific targets such as TermCounter, TermCounterTest, Index, and TestIndex. Separating compilation from execution helps distinguish compile-time problems from runtime or logic problems. If the source does not compile, the learner should first resolve syntax, type, or dependency errors before interpreting program output. Once compilation succeeds, the exercise target can reveal whether the implemented counting or indexing logic produces the expected behavior.
Study instruction:
- Follow the exercise sequence and record whether each failure occurs during compilation, program execution, or a test assertion.
Key point:
- Build first so the program is compiled before execution.
- Diagnose compile errors separately from incorrect algorithm results.
39. Q: Why might the order of terms printed by the index differ between program runs?
A: Show answer
The chapter warns that the order of terms may differ when the program runs. The implementation uses hash-based collections, whose iteration order should not be treated as a guaranteed presentation order.
